The cantons regulate the relationship between church and state.

abschnitte.text: **Article 15** of the Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and conscience. Every person may freely choose their **religion** or **world view**. They may profess it alone or with others. According to paragraph 4, nobody may be forced to join or belong to a religious community or to take part in a **religious act**.

Your **conscience** is the inner voice that tells you what is right and wrong. That is why Article 15 protects not only religious but also **philosophical convictions**. Even people who do not believe in any god are protected. So you may leave a church or not belong to any community at all. The state must remain **neutral** towards religions.

The Federal Constitution of **1848** only provided freedom of worship for the recognised Christian denominations. Only the constitution of **1874** guaranteed freedom of religion and conscience in general. At that time it was in **Article 49**. With the new constitution of 1999 it moved to Article 15. Its content stayed essentially the same.

abschnitte.titel: Church and state in the cantons
abschnitte.text: According to **Article 72 of the Federal Constitution**, the **cantons** regulate the relationship between church and state. That is why there are big differences. In many cantons certain churches are **recognised** under public law and may levy church taxes. Geneva and Neuchâtel separate church and state more strictly. But the Confederation makes sure that religious peace is maintained.

In the 19th century, the constitution still contained special bans on religious groups. One example is the **ban on the Jesuits**. It was removed from the Federal Constitution in a **popular vote in 1973**. At the same time, the ban on founding new monasteries was also dropped. These changes strengthened the equal treatment of religions.

gewusst: From the age of 16, young people in Switzerland may decide on their religious affiliation themselves.
Freedom of conscience was one reason why Switzerland introduced civilian service for those liable for military service.

teile.einleitung: Homework is tasks for school that you do at home. In German-speaking Switzerland many children call it “Ufzgi”. Homework helps you to practise and consolidate what you have learnt.
wichtigste: In Swiss German dialect, homework is often called “Ufzgi”.
Homework is mainly for practice.
You write down what you have to do in your homework diary.
A quiet place helps you to concentrate.
If you do not understand something, you ask.
Children do their homework themselves; parents may help.

abschnitte.text: In German-speaking Switzerland many children call their homework **“Ufzgi”**. The word comes from “Aufgaben”, meaning tasks. So that you do not forget anything, you write it in your **homework diary**. It also says when you have to do it by. The teacher tells you the **deadline**, and you keep to it.

Homework is mainly for **practice**. You go over what you have learnt at school. That way it stays in your head better. Sometimes you also prepare something for the next lesson, for example a short talk. Homework also helps you to work **independently** and to plan your time.

To do your homework well, you need a **quiet place**. There you can **concentrate** better. Loud noises, the television or your mobile phone are distracting. It also helps if everything you need is ready: exercise books, books and pens. Many children like to do their homework at the same time every day.

If you do not understand a task, **asking** is the best solution. You can ask your teacher, your parents or your brothers and sisters. Asking is allowed and good. Parents may help and explain. But **the child must do** the homework **themselves**, because that is the only way they learn something from it.

When your homework is finished, it goes into your **Schulthek**. That is what the school bag is called in Switzerland. It is best to pack your school bag the evening before. Then you will not forget anything in the morning. Some schools also offer **homework help**, where you can do your homework at school with support.

gewusst: Some schools in Switzerland do without homework completely or partly and do more practice in lessons instead.
In French-speaking Switzerland homework is called “les devoirs”.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who disagrees with a court judgement can often have it reviewed by a higher court. The sequence of courts is called the hierarchy of courts (Instanzenzug). In Switzerland it leads from the canton to the Federal Supreme Court.
wichtigste: The hierarchy of courts is the sequence of courts that examine a case.
In civil cases in Zurich, it leads from the district court via the high court to the Federal Supreme Court.
First-instance civil judgements with a value of 10,000 francs or more can be appealed.
In civil cases you can usually only go to the Federal Supreme Court if the amount in dispute is 30,000 francs or more.
In employment and tenancy cases, the limit is 15,000 francs.
Since 2007 there have been three unified appeals to the Federal Supreme Court.
After the Federal Supreme Court, a complaint in Strasbourg is possible.

abschnitte.text: A **hierarchy of courts** is like a staircase with several steps. Each step is a court, called an **instance**. In the canton of Zurich, in a civil case, after **conciliation** the **district court** examines the case first. After that you can go to the **high court** and finally to the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne. The Federal Supreme Court Act requires that, as a rule, the last cantonal instance is a **higher court**.

A route to a higher court is called a **legal remedy**. Against first-instance final decisions in civil cases with an amount in dispute of **10,000 francs** or more, there is an **appeal**. Below that, only an **objection** (Beschwerde) is possible. This is set out in the Swiss Civil Procedure Code. The higher instance then examines whether the first judgement was correct.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the Federal Supreme Court
abschnitte.text: The **Federal Supreme Court Act** of 2007 provides for three **unified appeals**: in civil cases, in criminal cases and in public-law matters. In civil cases there is usually a **threshold** of **30,000 francs** for the amount in dispute. In employment and tenancy cases it is lower, at **15,000 francs**. If the threshold is not reached, often only the **subsidiary constitutional complaint** remains. With it, you can only complain that constitutional rights have been violated.

The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland. Anyone who believes their **human rights** have been violated can then go to the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg. For this, the whole hierarchy of courts in Switzerland must first have been gone through. The Court only examines whether the **European Convention on Human Rights** has been violated. It is not an EU court but belongs to the Council of Europe.

gewusst: The Federal Supreme Court has its headquarters in Lausanne and a division in Lucerne.
Switzerland ratified the European Convention on Human Rights in 1974.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who gets enough votes in an election is elected. This marks the start of a new task, for example in the National Council or the Council of States. Different rules apply depending on the election.
wichtigste: Anyone elected to the National Council gets a seat in the chamber.
After the election, you must accept it.
If there are as many candidates as seats, this is called a tacit election.
If someone leaves the National Council, the next person on the list moves up.
Members of Parliament receive an allowance for their work.
An absolute majority means more than half of the votes.
With a relative majority, it is enough to have the most votes.

abschnitte.text: Anyone elected to the **National Council** gets a **seat** in the chamber. There are 200 seats in total. Those elected may speak in the chamber, make proposals and **vote**. The term of office is four years. At the start, the new members take an **oath** or make a **solemn promise**.

An elected person must first say whether they want to take up the office. They must **accept the election**. Only then do they take office. Sometimes someone declines, for example because they already hold another office that is not compatible. Then another person gets their turn.

If no more people stand than there are seats, nobody needs to vote. The candidates are then elected without a ballot. This is called a **tacit election**. If a member of the National Council resigns, there is no new election. Instead, the person who had the most votes on the same list but was not elected **moves up**.

With an **absolute majority**, you need more than half of the votes. This is usually needed in the first round of a **Council of States election**. If nobody manages this, there is a **second round**. There a **relative majority** is usually enough: whoever has more votes than everyone else is elected. You then no longer need half.

Members of the National Council receive an **allowance** for meetings and preparation. The Swiss Parliament is considered a **militia parliament**. Many members also have another job. In this way they bring experience from everyday life into politics. However, the office now takes up a lot of time.

gewusst: Tacit elections also happen in many municipalities, for example when exactly as many people stand for the municipal council as there are seats free.
The Council of States has 46 seats, the National Council 200.

teile.einleitung: Every Swiss canton has a capital. The cantonal government and usually also the cantonal parliament have their seat there. But the capital is not always the largest town in the canton.
wichtigste: The most important place in a canton is called its capital.
The cantonal government has its seat in the capital.
Many capitals have the same name as their canton, for example Lucerne or Zurich.
The capital of Thurgau is Frauenfeld.
The capital is not always the largest town in the canton.
Bern is Switzerland's federal city.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has **26 cantons**, and each has a **capital**. The **cantonal government** works there. The **cantonal parliament** usually meets there too, and many cantonal offices are based there. That is why the capital matters for the whole canton. Anyone who has business with the canton often travels there.

In several cantons the capital has the same name as the canton. The capital of the canton of **Lucerne** is Lucerne. **Zurich** is the capital of the canton of Zurich and also the largest city in Switzerland. Other examples are **Fribourg**, Bern, Zug, Schwyz, St Gallen and Geneva. The capital of **Basel-Stadt** is Basel, the city on the Rhine.

In other cantons the capital has its own name. The capital of **Thurgau** is **Frauenfeld**. In the canton of Aargau it is **Aarau**, in Valais **Sion**, in the Grisons **Chur** and in Ticino **Bellinzona**. In Uri it is **Altdorf**, in Obwalden Sarnen and in Nidwalden Stans.

The capital is the **seat of government**, not necessarily the largest town. In the canton of **Basel-Landschaft** the capital is **Liestal**. But the municipality of **Allschwil** is larger. In Ticino, too, Lugano is larger than the capital Bellinzona. In Valais, on the other hand, Sion is also the largest town.

For the whole country, **Bern** is the seat of the Federal Council and Parliament. Officially, however, Bern is called the **federal city**, not the capital. This is because the Constitution does not name a capital. Bern is also the capital of the **canton of Bern**. So the city has two important roles.

gewusst: In the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, the government and parliament sit in Herisau, but the high court sits in Trogen.
The old town of Fribourg is one of the largest medieval old towns in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Gender Equality Act, GlG for short, is a Swiss federal act. It aims to bring about equality between women and men, above all at work. It came into force on 1 July 1996.
wichtigste: The Gender Equality Act came into force on 1 July 1996.
It applies above all to working life.
It forbids discrimination in recruitment, pay, further training, promotion and dismissal.
In cases of pay discrimination, it is enough to show that it is likely.
Since 2020 larger employers have had to carry out an equal pay analysis.
Anyone who defends themselves is protected against dismissal in revenge.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Constitution says that men and women have equal rights. The **Gender Equality Act** puts this into concrete form for **working life**. It came into force on **1 July 1996**. The act forbids discrimination on grounds of sex in **recruitment**, **pay**, further training, promotion and dismissal. It applies to private and public employers.

Anyone who suspects they are paid less because of their sex often finds it hard to prove. That is why the act provides an **easier burden of proof**. The person concerned only has to **show that discrimination is likely**. Then the employer must prove that there is no discrimination. Harassment at work also counts as **discrimination** under the act, and employers must take preventive action.

Since the revision of **1 July 2020**, employers with at least **100 employees** must analyse their pay. The analysis must be checked independently. Employees are informed of the result. There are aids for this, such as the free pay analysis tool **Logib**. This is meant to make unfair pay differences visible.

Anyone who defends themselves against discrimination should not have to fear for their job. A dismissal in reaction to a complaint can be **challenged**. This protection applies during the proceedings and for **six months** afterwards. For disputes, there are **conciliation offices** in the cantons. There you can first try to reach an agreement.

The **Federal Office for Gender Equality**, FOGE for short (EBG in German), works to put the act into practice. It provides information, gives advice and supports projects. It also provides tools such as **Logib**. Many cantons and cities also have their own **equality offices**.

gewusst: The Gender Equality Act came exactly 15 years after the vote on the equality article of 1981.
The duty to carry out an equal pay analysis is time-limited and, as things stand, applies until 2032.

teile.einleitung: A court is a place where justice is administered. There, judges decide disputes and examine whether someone has broken a law. By the way, the German word “Gericht” can also mean a dish of food.
wichtigste: In court, judges decide according to the law.
A person accused of a crime is called the defendant.
Witnesses say what they have seen or heard.
A case is discussed at a hearing.
Many judgements can be taken to a higher court.
In Switzerland, juvenile criminal law applies from the age of 10.
Many hearings are public.

abschnitte.text: A **court** decides when people have a dispute or when someone is said to have done something forbidden. The **judges** listen to all sides and examine the evidence. At the end they give a **judgement** according to the law. The German word “Gericht” has two meanings: it can also be a dish on a plate.

The meeting in court at which a case is discussed is called a **hearing**. The person accused of a crime is the **defendant**. A lawyer can defend them. **Witnesses** say what they have seen or heard and must tell the truth. Until the judgement, every person is presumed innocent.

In Switzerland there are courts at several **levels**. First, a court in the district or region usually decides. Anyone who disagrees with the judgement can take it to a **higher court**. This examines the case again. At the very top is the **Federal Supreme Court**, based in Lausanne.

For children and young people there is a special **juvenile criminal law**. In Switzerland it applies from the age of **10**. Younger children are not punished. The **juvenile court** is mainly about education and protection. Young people should learn from their mistake and find a good path again.

Many court hearings in Switzerland are **public**. So spectators may attend. That way everyone can see that decisions are made fairly. Journalists also often report on court cases. For young people, or to protect those involved, a hearing can also take place without an audience.

gewusst: The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland; part of it works in Lucerne.
Anyone who deliberately lies as a witness in court can be punished themselves.

teile.einleitung: A municipal coat of arms is the identifying sign of a municipality. Almost every Swiss municipality has its own coat of arms with colours and pictures that often tell a story.
wichtigste: Coats of arms have existed since the Middle Ages.
The study of coats of arms is called heraldry.
Canting arms show a picture that matches the place name.
The city of St Gallen has a bear with a golden collar in its coat of arms.
Chur shows an ibex in a town gate, Winterthur two red lions.
The coat of arms of Rapperswil-Jona has roses.

abschnitte.text: The first **coats of arms** appeared around 900 years ago in the **Middle Ages**. Knights carried them on their shields so that they could be recognised. Later, towns and villages also adopted such signs. The study of how coats of arms are designed and described is called **heraldry**.

Some coats of arms show a picture that matches the place name. They are called **canting arms**, because the picture “speaks” the name. **Schaffhausen** shows a **ram** (Schafbock). In the coat of arms of **Frauenfeld**, a **woman** (Frau) holds a red lion on a golden chain. And in **Rapperswil-Jona** the **roses** recall Rapperswil, the “town of roses”, together with a blue wavy line.

Many coats of arms show animals. The **city of St Gallen** has an upright **bear** with a golden collar, which Emperor Frederick III allowed in 1475. In **Chur** a black **ibex** stands in a red town gate on a silver background. **Winterthur** shows a red diagonal band on silver, with **two red lions** striding beside it.

It is not only animals that appear. The coat of arms of **Biel/Bienne** shows **two silver crossed axes** on a red background. **Olten** has **three green fir trees** on a green triple mound and has used this coat of arms since 1653 at the latest. Municipal coats of arms can be seen on flags, letters, municipal halls and often at village festivals.

gewusst: The bear in the St Gallen coat of arms got its golden collar from an emperor in 1475.
In heraldry, yellow and white are often called gold and silver.

teile.einleitung: Hannah Arendt was an important political thinker of the 20th century. She lived from 1906 to 1975 and, as a Jew, had to flee Germany. In her books she thought about power, freedom and totalitarian rule.
wichtigste: Hannah Arendt lived from 1906 to 1975.
She wrote her doctoral thesis under Karl Jaspers.
In 1933 she fled Germany; in 1951 she became a citizen of the USA.
Her main work is called “The Origins of Totalitarianism”.
She coined the expression “banality of evil” in her report on the Eichmann trial.
She distinguished between labour, work and action.
For her, power comes about through acting together.

abschnitte.text: Hannah Arendt was born near Hanover in 1906 and grew up in Königsberg. She studied **philosophy**. In 1928 she wrote her doctoral thesis in Heidelberg under **Karl Jaspers**. From 1948 Jaspers later taught at the University of **Basel**. As a Jew, Arendt fled Germany in **1933**. In 1937 the Nazis stripped her of her citizenship; until 1951 she was **stateless**, and after that a citizen of the USA.

In **1951** her main work, **“The Origins of Totalitarianism”**, was published. In it she examines National Socialism and Stalinism. She describes how **antisemitism** and imperialism paved the way. For her, the hallmarks of **totalitarianism** are **terror and ideology**. Such a state wants to control people's whole lives.

In **1961** Arendt watched the trial of **Adolf Eichmann** in **Jerusalem**. He shared responsibility for organising the persecution and murder of Jews. To her, Eichmann seemed not a demon but a **thoughtless bureaucrat**. For this she coined the expression **“banality of evil”**. Her report sparked great debates that continue to this day.

In **“The Human Condition”** Arendt distinguishes three activities: **labour** secures survival, and **work** creates lasting things. For her, only **action** among people is political in the true sense. Its basic condition is **plurality**, meaning the diversity of people. In **“On Violence”** she stresses: **power** comes about when people join together. Violence can destroy power, but not create it.

In her book **“On Revolution”**, Arendt compares the **American** and the **French** Revolutions. She considers the American Revolution more successful. In her view it created lasting institutions of freedom, for example a constitution. The French Revolution, by contrast, failed because of the **social question**, meaning poverty and hardship.

gewusst: Arendt did not see herself as a philosopher but as a political theorist.
For decades she exchanged letters with her teacher Karl Jaspers, which were later published as a book.

teile.einleitung: In a secret election or vote, nobody knows how a person voted. That way everyone can decide freely, without being afraid of others.
wichtigste: In a secret vote, you write your choice on a ballot paper.
You fold the paper so that nobody can read it.
The ballot papers are collected in a ballot box.
You do not write your own name on the paper.
Each person has exactly one vote.
Papers that cannot be read are invalid.

abschnitte.text: If nobody can see how you vote, you do not need to be afraid that others will be angry or laugh at you. You can honestly choose what you yourself want. That is why the **secret ballot** is an important principle of democracy. You can vote this way in class too, for example when electing a class representative.

Each person gets exactly **one ballot paper**, because each person has one vote. You write your choice on it **clearly**. You do not add your **own name**, otherwise people would know who voted that way. Then you **fold** the paper so that nobody can read it. You also do not look at other people's papers and you do not show your own.

You put the folded papers into a **ballot box**, a box with a slot. They stay there until everyone has voted. Then they are counted. A paper on which nothing can be made out is **invalid** and does not count.

In Switzerland many people vote **by post** and send their ballot paper in an envelope. Anyone who goes to the ballot box will find booths or screens at the **polling station**, where they can fill in their paper undisturbed. One exception is the **Landsgemeinde** in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden: there people vote openly by raising their hands.

gewusst: At the Landsgemeinde, everyone can see how their neighbours vote.
In German, the box for ballot papers has the same name, “Urne”, as the vessel for ashes.

teile.einleitung: In a municipal merger, two or more municipalities join together to form a new municipality. In Switzerland this has happened often in recent decades.
wichtigste: In a municipal merger, several municipalities become one.
Voters vote on a merger.
After a merger there are fewer municipalities, but the villages remain.
In 2011 the canton of Glarus merged its 25 municipalities into three.
Mergers usually come into effect on 1 January.
Around 1850 Switzerland had 3203 municipalities.

abschnitte.text: In a **municipal merger**, two or more municipalities join together. The previous municipalities then no longer exist; there is only one new one. But the **villages** with their houses stay where they are. What is combined is mainly the **administration**, the municipal council and the finances. The new municipality often gets a **new name**; sometimes it keeps an old one.

Small municipalities sometimes find it hard to find people for public offices. Tasks such as schools, water supply or building control are also becoming more and more demanding. Together, municipalities can **carry out these tasks better** and save money. Opponents, on the other hand, fear that people will have less say and that a village will lose its independence.

As a rule, the **voters** of the municipalities involved vote on a merger. If all say yes, the merger is prepared. It usually comes into effect on **1 January**, so that the new municipality can start with its own budget.

abschnitte.titel: Glarus and the whole of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: A particularly big step was taken in the **canton of Glarus**: in 2011 its 25 municipalities were merged into just three. They are called **Glarus**, **Glarus Nord** and **Glarus Süd**. In 1850, shortly after the founding of the federal state, there were **3203 municipalities** in Switzerland. Since then the number has fallen sharply because of mergers.

gewusst: Since 2011 Glarus has had fewer municipalities than almost any other canton.
After a merger, a village can still keep its name as a district.

teile.einleitung: In a show of hands, people vote by raising their hand. This is how decisions are made at many municipal assemblies and at the Landsgemeinde. The method is simple, open and quick.
wichtigste: In a show of hands, you raise your hand to vote.
First people are asked for the yes votes, then for the no votes.
Each person votes only for themselves.
Guests may watch but may not vote.
Vote counters count the hands, especially when it is close.
Before the vote you may give your opinion and make proposals.

abschnitte.titel: How a show of hands works
abschnitte.text: In a **show of hands**, people vote with a raised hand. The chair first asks: who is in favour? Then everyone voting **yes** raises their hand. Next the chair asks for the **no votes**, and the others raise their hand. You keep your hand up until the votes have been **counted**. At the **Landsgemeinde**, the Landammann asks in this way.

In many Swiss municipalities the **municipal assembly** decides important questions. Before the vote, you can ask to speak and **give your opinion**. Every voter may also make a **proposal** of their own. Then the assembly votes on it. That way everyone hears what speaks for or against something.

Only **people entitled to vote** may vote. Each person votes **only for themselves**. So you may not raise your hand for a friend who is ill. Guests may watch but sit in special **guest seats**. In some municipalities voters receive a **voting card** at the entrance, which they hold up when voting.

The **vote counters** count the raised hands. With 3 rows of 12 hands each, for example, there are 36 hands. If 52 people raise their hand for yes and 38 for no, yes has 14 hands more. If the result is clear, there is no need to count exactly. The vote counters are especially important when it is **close**. Then every vote counts.

A show of hands is an **open vote**: everyone can see how the others vote. This is quick and transparent. But some people think it can create pressure. That is why an assembly can often also decide to hold a **secret vote**. In votes at the ballot box, your vote always remains secret.

gewusst: Landsgemeinden with a show of hands still exist today in the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
At the Landsgemeinde the crowd is often so large that the Landammann can only estimate the majority.

teile.einleitung: The Habeas Corpus Act is an English law of 1679. It protects people from being locked up without reason and without a trial. The idea behind it applies in many countries today, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The English Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act in 1679.
It protects against arbitrary arrest.
“Habeas corpus” literally means: you shall have the body.
It was passed under King Charles II.
Abraham Lincoln partly suspended this right in 1861.
In Switzerland the idea is found in Article 31 of the Federal Constitution.
Article 5 of the ECHR also protects the right to have detention reviewed.

abschnitte.text: In **1679** the **English Parliament** passed the Habeas Corpus Act. The law set out more precisely an older legal remedy against **arbitrary detention**. The king at the time was **Charles II**, who reigned after the restoration of the monarchy. Parliament wanted to prevent the Crown from having people locked up as it pleased. The law is considered a milestone in the protection of personal freedom.

The Latin phrase **“habeas corpus”** literally means **“you shall have the body”**. It comes from the order to the jailer. He had to bring the prisoner **in person before the court**. The court then examined whether the detention was **lawful**. If it was not, the person was set free.

The core of the law is simple: nobody should be held for as long as someone likes without reason and without proceedings. Detention must be **reviewed quickly**. This idea is an important basis of the **rule of law**. It later influenced many constitutions and declarations of human rights, for example in the USA.

The **US Constitution** protects the right of habeas corpus. It only allows it to be suspended in cases of **rebellion or invasion**. During the **Civil War**, President **Abraham Lincoln** had the right suspended in parts of Maryland in April 1861. He wanted to prevent sabotage against the Union. This step was very controversial at the time.

In Switzerland **Article 31 of the Federal Constitution** regulates deprivation of liberty. Anyone taken into **pre-trial detention** has the right to be brought before a court without delay. The **European Convention on Human Rights** also protects this right. **Article 5 ECHR** lists the permitted reasons for detention exhaustively. Every person who is arrested has the right to a **review by a court**.

gewusst: Even the Magna Carta of 1215 contained the idea that nobody may be imprisoned without a lawful judgement.
In many countries, the term habeas corpus is still used today as the name for the right to have detention reviewed.

teile.einleitung: Inclusion means that all people belong and can take part. This also applies to people with a disability. Instead of someone having to adapt, the surroundings are designed so that they suit everyone.
wichtigste: With inclusion, everyone belongs and nobody is left out.
Blind people often read braille with their fingers.
A braille character has at most six dots.
Many deaf people communicate in sign language.
Ramps and lifts make buildings accessible for wheelchairs.
Athletes with disabilities compete at the Paralympics.
The International Day of Persons with Disabilities is on 3 December.

abschnitte.text: **Inclusion** comes from the Latin word for “to shut in” or include. All people should be able to take part at school, at work and in their free time. This concerns people with a **disability** in particular. Often even a small change helps everyone to take part. If a child in a wheelchair wants to join in, you can adapt the game so that they are included.

Many blind people read **braille**. It consists of raised dots that you feel with your fingers. Each character has room for **six dots** in two rows. It was invented by the Frenchman **Louis Braille**, who was blind himself. When walking, a white cane or a specially trained **guide dog** helps.

Many deaf people communicate in **sign language**. You speak with your hands, face and body. Sign languages are languages in their own right, with their own grammar. In German-speaking Switzerland there is **Swiss German Sign Language**; in French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino there are others. For some television programmes, interpreters translate into sign language.

Stairs are an obstacle for people in a **wheelchair**. **Ramps**, lifts and wide doors make buildings accessible for everyone. In Switzerland the **Disability Discrimination Act** has applied since 2004, and in 2014 Switzerland joined the **UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities**. In sport, athletes with disabilities compete at the **Paralympics**, which take place shortly after the Olympic Games. On **3 December**, a UN day draws attention to the rights of people with disabilities.

gewusst: Louis Braille developed his script when he was still a teenager.
On many medicine packets, the name is also written in braille.

teile.einleitung: With municipal tax, a municipality pays for many tasks that benefit everyone. In Switzerland each municipality decides for itself how high its tax is.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people pay taxes to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality.
With taxes, the municipality pays for schools, roads, the fire brigade and more.
Taxes are paid by adults with income or assets and by companies.
Those who earn more pay more tax.
The tax rate determines how high the municipal tax is.
Each municipality has its own tax rate.

abschnitte.text: The municipality has many tasks. It builds and runs **schools**, maintains **roads** and organises the **fire brigade**. For this it needs money, which comes mainly from **taxes**. State schools in Switzerland are free of charge. Exercise books and school materials are also paid for with taxes, so everyone pays for school together.

In Switzerland people pay taxes in **three places**: to the **Confederation**, the **canton** and the **municipality**. Each uses them to pay for its own tasks. Taxes are paid mainly by **adults** who earn money or have assets. **Companies** pay taxes too. Children without their own income do not pay any.

Every year adults fill in a **tax return**. In it they write down how much they earn and own. From this, the amount of tax they pay is calculated. Those who **earn more** pay more tax; those who earn little pay less. That way each person contributes according to their means.

Each municipality sets its own **tax rate**. This number shows how high the municipal tax is. A low tax rate means less tax. In many municipalities it is decided by the **voters** at the municipal assembly or by the municipal parliament. That is why people pay more or less tax depending on where they live.

gewusst: Two families with the same income can pay different amounts of tax depending on their municipality.
In many municipalities, voters decide themselves how high their tax is.

teile.einleitung: On the desk of the President of the National Council stands a small bell. The person chairing the chamber uses it to get attention. The bell is a sign of who is leading the meeting.
wichtigste: A small hand bell stands on the President's desk.
With the bell, the chair asks for quiet and attention.
A session is traditionally opened with the ring of the bell.
The president is elected anew every year.
The person at the head of the National Council is often called the highest Swiss citizen.
If there is a tie, the President has the casting vote.

abschnitte.text: In the National Council chamber, the **President of the National Council** sits at the front at a raised desk. A small **hand bell** stands there. When it gets too noisy in the chamber, the President rings the bell. In this way she asks for **quiet** and attention. The bell works better than shouting.

Parliament meets for **sessions**, normally four times a year for three weeks. At the beginning, the President traditionally rings the bell. In this way the session is **rung in**. Individual meetings or votes are also often announced with the ring of the bell.

The President **chairs the meeting**. She gives members the floor, keeps an eye on speaking time and guides the chamber through the **votes**. Normally she does not vote herself. But if there is a tie, her vote decides. This is called the **casting vote**.

The person at the head of the National Council is often called the **“highest Swiss woman”** or **“highest Swiss man”**. In terms of protocol, the office comes right at the top, even ahead of the Federal Council. The President is elected for **one year** at a time. That way different people and parties take their turn. Re-election the following year is not planned.

At the start of the **2020 spring session**, the little bell had suddenly disappeared. The President of the National Council, **Isabelle Moret**, knew what to do. She **clapped her hands** to get quiet. This little story shows how much the bell is part of the chamber's work.

gewusst: The President of the National Council also chairs the United Federal Assembly, for example when the Federal Council is elected.
The Council of States also has a presidency that changes every year.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the word Gemeinderat does not mean the same thing everywhere. In most municipalities it is the government, but in some towns it is the parliament.
wichtigste: In most small municipalities the Gemeinderat is the executive.
It usually consists of five to nine people.
It is led by the mayor, called Gemeindeammann in some cantons.
In the city of Zurich the Gemeinderat is the parliament and the Stadtrat is the government.
In the city of Bern it is the other way round.
Elections are usually held under the majority system.

abschnitte.text: In most small Swiss municipalities the **Gemeinderat** (municipal council) is the **executive**, meaning the government. It runs the municipality and carries out decisions. It usually has **five to nine members**, and each is responsible for certain areas. It is elected by the municipality's **voters**, at the ballot box or at the municipal assembly.

One member leads the Gemeinderat. In many municipalities this person is called the **mayor** (Gemeindepräsidentin or Gemeindepräsident). They chair the meetings and represent the municipality to the outside world. Depending on the canton the office has a different name; in Aargau, for example, it is **Gemeindeammann** or Stadtammann. But the task is the same.

In the **city of Zurich** the **Stadtrat** is the government, while the Gemeinderat is the **parliament**. In the **city of Bern** it is the other way round: there the government is called the Gemeinderat, and the parliament with 80 seats is called the **Stadtrat**. So when you hear these terms, you always need to know which town is meant.

In small municipalities the councillors usually work **part-time**, alongside their job. This is called the **militia system**. In big towns the office is a full-time job. Elections are usually held under the **majority system**: the people with the most votes are elected. Some towns such as **Bern** or **Biel**, by contrast, elect their executive by **proportional representation**, meaning according to the parties' share of the vote.

gewusst: The same word means the parliament in Zurich and the government in Bern.
The militia system is considered typically Swiss.

teile.einleitung: The pedestrian crossing, also called a zebra crossing, helps you to cross the road safely. In Switzerland it is yellow and there are clear rules.
wichtigste: In Switzerland zebra crossings are yellow.
The name comes from the stripes, like those of a zebra.
At a zebra crossing without traffic lights, pedestrians have priority over cars.
Trams have priority even at zebra crossings.
A saying to remember: “Wheel stops, child goes.”
You walk briskly, but you do not run.

abschnitte.text: A **pedestrian crossing** consists of wide bars painted on the road. Because they look like a **zebra's** coat, it is also called a **zebra crossing**. In Switzerland they are painted **yellow**, while in many other countries they are white. At a zebra crossing, drivers expect pedestrians. That is why it is the safest place to cross the road, not between parked cars or on bends.

At a zebra crossing without traffic lights, **pedestrians have priority**. Cars must stop when someone wants to cross the road. One exception is the **tram**: it cannot swerve and brakes only slowly. That is why it has priority even at zebra crossings. If there are traffic lights, the light signal applies.

Before you set off, you stop at the kerb and look left, right and left again. If a car is coming, remember the saying **“Wheel stops, child goes”**. Only when the wheels have come to a complete stop is it safe. It also helps to make eye contact with the driver. Then you walk **briskly**, but you do not run, because if you run you can trip or not be seen.

On wide roads there is often a **traffic island** in the middle. You can wait there safely. That way you only have to watch one lane and one direction of traffic at a time. This makes crossing easier and safer.

gewusst: Yellow pedestrian crossings are rather rare in Europe.
In Switzerland trams have priority even at zebra crossings.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetic Republic existed from 1798 to 1803. It came about when French troops occupied the old Confederation. For the first time, Switzerland was a unitary state with a shared government.
wichtigste: The Helvetic Republic was proclaimed in Aarau on 12 April 1798.
It was a unitary state; the cantons were only administrative districts.
The first constitution was written by Peter Ochs from Basel, based on the French model.
The government was a Directory with five members.
The subject territories were abolished, and all citizens received equal rights.
The national colours were green, red and yellow.
After the Stecklikrieg of 1802, the republic collapsed.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 18th century, the **French Revolution** changed the whole of Europe. In 1798 French troops marched into the old Confederation. On **12 April 1798**, 121 representatives in **Aarau** proclaimed the Helvetic Republic. Aarau became the first, provisional capital. The constitution had been written by **Peter Ochs** from Basel on behalf of France.

The republic was a **unitary state**. A central government ran the whole country. The cantons lost their **sovereignty** and became administrative districts, each headed by a **government prefect**. The government was called the **Directory** and, as in France, had five members. Parliament consisted of the Senate and the Grand Council.

The constitution brought big changes. The **subject territories** were abolished, and all citizens received **equal rights**. There was now freedom of religion and freedom of the press. The national colours were **green, red and yellow**. Many of these ideas came back later in the federal state of 1848.

Not everyone wanted the new state. **Nidwalden** rejected the constitution, and on 9 September 1798 French troops crushed the uprising. Many people were killed. For the orphans, **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi** set up an orphanage in **Stans** on behalf of the government. In 1802 opponents drove out the Helvetic troops in the **Stecklikrieg**, and in 1803 Napoleon ended the republic with the **Act of Mediation**.

gewusst: The Stecklikrieg (war of sticks) got its name because many of the rebels were armed only with clubs.
Pestalozzi described his experiences in Stans in the famous “Stans letter”.

teile.einleitung: The Hagenbach-Bischoff method is a way of distributing seats among parties in proportional elections. It is named after the Basel physicist Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff. In Switzerland it is used, for example, in National Council elections.
wichtigste: Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff (1833 to 1910) was a physicist from Basel.
He campaigned for proportional representation.
First you calculate the distribution number: votes divided by seats plus one, rounded up.
Each party gets as many seats as the number of times the distribution number fits fully into its votes.
Remaining seats go to the party with the highest figure of votes divided by seats plus one.
The result is always the same as with the D'Hondt method.
Large parties have a slight advantage.

abschnitte.text: **Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff** lived from 1833 to 1910. He was a Swiss **physicist** and professor in **Basel**. Besides science, he was interested in politics. He campaigned for **proportional representation**, in which seats are distributed according to the share of the vote. For this he developed a method of calculation that now bears his name.

First you count all the valid **party votes**. You divide these by the number of **seats plus one**. The next highest whole number is the **distribution number**. Example: 5 seats and 10,000 votes. 10,000 divided by 6 is 1666.67, so the distribution number is **1667**. Each party gets as many seats as the number of times the distribution number fits fully into its votes. Party A with 4000 votes first gets 2 seats, because 4000 divided by 1667 is 2.4.

Often there are seats left over after the first distribution. Then each party divides its votes by its current **seats plus one**. The party with the highest figure gets the **remaining seat**. Example: A has 4000 votes and 2 seats, B 3000 and 1 seat, C 2000 and 1 seat, D 1000 and no seat. The figures are A 1333, B 1500, C 1000 and D 1000. The last seat goes to **B**.

The Hagenbach-Bischoff method is just another way of calculating the **D'Hondt method**. Both distribute the seats in **exactly the same way**. As with D'Hondt, **large parties** often get a small advantage with the remaining seats. That is why smaller parties often link their lists. Such a **list alliance** is first treated like a single party in the distribution.

In **National Council elections** the method is used in the cantons with several seats. The National Council has been elected by proportional representation since **1919**. Many cantons and municipalities also use the method. However, some cantons have switched to the **double Pukelsheim** for their parliamentary elections. This distributes the seats more precisely according to the share of the vote.

gewusst: With only 2 seats, a party with 6000 of 10,000 votes can win both seats if the others have 2500 and 1500 votes.
The D'Hondt method is named after the Belgian lawyer Victor D'Hondt.

teile.einleitung: On 26 November 1989 Switzerland voted on a popular initiative that wanted to abolish the army. It was rejected but received many more yes votes than expected. The vote set off a big debate about the role of the army.
wichtigste: The initiative came from the Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSoA).
The GSoA was founded in 1982.
In 1989, 35.6 per cent of voters said yes.
The Federal Council and Parliament clearly rejected the initiative.
The Federal Council based its no on armed neutrality.
Most young voters said yes, older voters clearly said no.
A second attempt in 2001 received only around 22 per cent yes.

abschnitte.text: The **Group for a Switzerland without an Army**, **GSoA** for short, was founded in 1982 in the setting of the peace movement. It wanted to abolish the army and promote a comprehensive peace policy. For this it launched a **popular initiative** and collected the necessary signatures. For many people, even the idea broke a taboo. On 26 November 1989 the initiative went to the ballot box.

The **Federal Council** rejected the initiative. It relied on **armed neutrality**: Switzerland should be able to protect its neutrality militarily. In the **National Council** the rejection was very clear, by 172 votes to 13. The **Council of States** even rejected it unanimously. There was no counter-proposal.

With **35.6 per cent yes**, just over a third of voters said yes. This was far above the expectations of the Federal Council and the initiators. The cantons of **Jura** and **Geneva** even approved the initiative. According to a follow-up survey, most **under-30s** voted yes, while the over-60s very clearly voted no. There were also big differences between the parties: 91 per cent of SVP and FDP supporters rejected it, while there were yes majorities among SP and Green supporters.

Well-known writers such as **Max Frisch** and **Friedrich Dürrenmatt** publicly supported the initiative. Max Frisch wrote the text “Switzerland without an army? A palaver” about it. After the vote, the army was reformed and reduced in size over the following years. A **second attempt** by the GSoA clearly failed in December 2001, with around 78 per cent voting no. The GSoA still campaigns for its goals today with further initiatives.

gewusst: The 1989 vote took place only a few weeks after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Turnout in 1989 was unusually high, at around 69 per cent.

teile.einleitung: Fundamental rights are the most important rights that every person has. In Switzerland they are set out in the Federal Constitution. They protect all people, including children, from injustice and arbitrary action by the state.
wichtigste: Fundamental rights are important rights for all people.
They are set out in the Federal Constitution.
The fundamental rights begin with human dignity in Article 7.
All people are equal before the law.
Children and young people are entitled to special protection.
Freedom of religion and freedom of assembly are fundamental rights.
Anyone in need is entitled to help with the bare essentials.

abschnitte.text: **Fundamental rights** are the most important rights that every person has. They are set out in the **Federal Constitution** and protect everyone. The state must respect them. Right at the beginning is **human dignity** in Article 7: human dignity must be respected and protected. Then comes **equality before the law**: all people are equal before the law.

**Article 11** of the Federal Constitution says that children and young people are **specially protected** and supported. They should be able to develop well. In addition, all children have a right to free **primary education**. The **right to privacy** also applies to children: it protects, for example, their home, their letters and their personal data.

Many fundamental rights are **freedoms**. **Freedom of religion** allows every person to decide for themselves whether and what they believe. **Freedom of expression** allows you to say what you think. **Freedom of assembly** allows people to meet peacefully, for example for a demonstration. And **academic freedom** in Article 20 protects research and teaching.

**Freedom of establishment** allows Swiss citizens to live anywhere in the country. So you may freely choose which municipality you live in. Anyone who is in need and cannot help themselves has a **right to assistance in situations of need**. This includes food, shelter and medical care.

Fundamental rights do not apply without limits. But they may only be **restricted** under strict conditions. There must be a legal basis and a **public interest**, and the restriction must be **proportionate**. The core of a fundamental right may never be touched. Anyone who feels their fundamental rights have been violated can turn to a **court**.

gewusst: The current Federal Constitution has applied since 1 January 2000 and contains 30 articles on fundamental rights.
The European Convention on Human Rights also protects fundamental rights and has applied in Switzerland since 1974.

teile.einleitung: Hospitality means welcoming visitors in a friendly way so that they feel at home. Children can be good hosts and polite guests too.
wichtigste: You greet visitors in a friendly way, for example with “Welcome!”.
You offer a guest something to drink.
A good host shares their toys.
Before someone comes to visit, you ask your parents.
When you leave, you say thank you for the invitation.

abschnitte.text: When visitors are at the door, you say **“Welcome!”** and ask them in. Their jacket is hung up on the **coat rack** by the entrance. In many Swiss homes people take off their **shoes** when they come in, so that the floor stays clean. You often first offer the guest **something to drink**, for example water, squash or tea.

Before a friend comes round to play, you ask your **parents** whether it suits them. When your friend is there, you **share** your toys. That way you both have fun. If you have played together, you can also **tidy up together**, so that one person does not have to do everything alone.

There are rules for guests too. If something gets broken at someone's house, you **say so honestly** and apologise. Then you can find a solution together. When you leave, you say **“Thank you for having me”**. This shows that you enjoyed the visit.

Hospitality is important in almost all cultures of the world. But the customs are different. In some countries guests are always offered tea; elsewhere the guest brings a small present. If you ask with curiosity, you learn a lot about other cultures.

gewusst: The word “Garderobe” (cloakroom) comes from French and originally meant a room for clothes.
In many cultures it is considered a great honour to host guests.

teile.einleitung: A municipal parliament is the elected representative body of a municipality. Larger towns in particular have such a parliament, while many small municipalities decide at the municipal assembly.
wichtigste: Town parliaments are usually elected by proportional representation.
The names differ depending on the place and the language.
In Bern the town parliament has 80 members, in Winterthur 60.
In Geneva, Lausanne and Ticino, the authorities have French or Italian names.
Article 50 of the Federal Constitution protects municipal autonomy.
Neuchâtel has had voting rights for foreigners at municipal level since 1849.

abschnitte.text: In most small Swiss municipalities, voters decide at the **municipal assembly**. Larger municipalities and towns, on the other hand, have a **municipal parliament**. Its members are elected by the people and decide, for example, on the budget and regulations. Alongside it is the **executive**, the government of the municipality. Almost everywhere, parliaments are elected by **proportional representation**, so parties receive seats in proportion to their votes.

The names are confusingly varied. In **Winterthur** the parliament is called the **Grosser Gemeinderat** and has 60 members, while the government is called the Stadtrat. In **Lucerne** the parliament is called the **Grosser Stadtrat** and the five-member government the Stadtrat. In **Bern** it is the other way round: the parliament with **80 members** is called the Stadtrat. It is elected every four years.

In the **city of Geneva**, the **Conseil administratif** with five members runs the city, and the parliament is called the Conseil municipal. In **Lausanne** the **Municipalité** with seven members forms the government, and the parliament is called the Conseil communal. In **Ticino** the **Municipio** runs the municipality, led by the Sindaco. There the parliament is called the Consiglio comunale.

**Article 50** of the Federal Constitution guarantees **municipal autonomy**, but its extent depends on cantonal law. The Confederation must take into account the effects of its actions on the municipalities. The cantons also decide who may vote. The canton of **Neuchâtel** has had voting rights for foreigners at municipal level since as early as **1849**. Today several cantons in French-speaking Switzerland have similar rules.

gewusst: In the city of Bern the government is called the Gemeinderat and the parliament the Stadtrat.
Neuchâtel introduced voting rights for foreigners in its municipalities shortly after the founding of the federal state.

teile.einleitung: A counter-proposal is Parliament's response to a popular initiative. It takes up the aim but often goes less far than the initiative.
wichtigste: A counter-proposal is also called a counter-draft.
It is drawn up by Parliament, the Federal Assembly.
A counter-proposal is voluntary.
With a direct counter-proposal, you vote on both proposals at the same time.
Since 1987 you may say yes twice; the deciding question settles it.
An indirect counter-proposal usually changes a law.

abschnitte.text: With a **popular initiative**, citizens can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. Parliament can respond with a **counter-proposal**, also called a **counter-draft**. It often does this when it likes the idea but thinks the initiative goes too far. The counter-proposal is then usually milder. It is not compulsory: many initiatives go to the vote without a counter-proposal.

A **direct counter-proposal** also changes the Constitution. That is why the initiative and the counter-proposal are voted on on the same day. An **indirect counter-proposal** usually changes a **law** instead of the Constitution. The people do not vote on it together with the initiative. But a referendum can be called against it.

Since a vote in **1987**, you may say **yes twice** to the initiative and the direct counter-proposal. In addition, there is the **deciding question**: you state which proposal you would prefer if both are approved. This gives a clear result in the end. Because it is about the Constitution, a **majority of the people** and a **majority of the cantons** are needed.

If the **initiative committee** likes the counter-proposal, it can **withdraw** its initiative. With a direct counter-draft, only the counter-draft then goes to the vote, because as a change to the Constitution it is subject to the **mandatory referendum**. With an indirect counter-proposal, a committee often only withdraws its initiative on condition that the counter-proposal comes into force.

gewusst: Before 1987 a double yes was counted as invalid.
Sometimes a committee achieves more with a counter-proposal than it would have achieved with the initiative at the ballot box.

teile.einleitung: The House of Lords is the upper house of the Parliament of the United Kingdom. Unlike the House of Commons, it is not elected by the people. It examines laws and can delay them, but usually cannot stop them.
wichtigste: The House of Lords is the second chamber of the British Parliament.
Its members are not elected by the people.
26 bishops of the Church of England sit there as Lords Spiritual.
Since 1999 most hereditary peers have no longer had a seat.
The upper house can only delay most laws.
Since 2006 the Lord Speaker has chaired the sittings.
Since 2009 the Supreme Court has been the highest court.

abschnitte.text: The British Parliament has two chambers: the elected **House of Commons** and the **House of Lords**. Both sit in the Palace of Westminster in London. The Lords are not elected but are mostly appointed for life. Many of them are experts from science, business or politics. The chamber examines laws closely and proposes changes.

The 26 bishops of the **Church of England** are called the **Lords Spiritual**. They include the Archbishops of Canterbury and York. All the other members are called **Lords Temporal**. In the past, many nobles had an inherited right to a seat. The **House of Lords Act 1999** took away the seats of most **hereditary peers**; only 92 were allowed to stay for the time being, and a newer law also ends their right to sit.

Since the **Parliament Acts** of 1911 and 1949, the upper house can only **delay** most laws. It can hold up normal laws for about a year, and money bills for only a month. After that, the House of Commons can pass them on its own. Under the **Salisbury Convention**, the Lords do not block laws that the governing party announced in its election manifesto. This rule dates from 1945.

The person presiding sits on the **Woolsack**, a large cushion stuffed with wool. It is a reminder of how important the **wool trade** was for England in the Middle Ages. In the past, the Lord Chancellor, a member of the government, chaired the sittings. Since **2006** the Lords have elected their own **Lord Speaker**. Until 2009 the House of Lords was also the highest court; then the **Supreme Court of the United Kingdom** took over.

gewusst: Today the Woolsack is stuffed with wool from several Commonwealth countries.
The House of Lords is one of the largest parliamentary chambers in the world.

teile.einleitung: Gerrymandering is the deliberate drawing of constituency boundaries so that one party wins more seats. With the same number of votes, a completely different result can come out. The practice is best known from the USA.
wichtigste: In gerrymandering, constituencies are drawn to favour one party.
The name comes from Elbridge Gerry and the word salamander.
In cracking, the opponents are spread over many constituencies.
In packing, the opponents are squeezed into a few constituencies.
In the USA, constituencies are redrawn after every census, every 10 years.
Some states, such as California, let an independent commission draw the boundaries.

abschnitte.text: In 1812 **Elbridge Gerry**, Governor of Massachusetts, signed a law on new electoral districts. One of them had a very twisted shape and helped his party. A newspaper compared it to a **salamander**. Gerry and salamander became the word **gerrymander**. Gerry later even became Vice-President of the USA.

There are two main techniques. In **cracking**, the opponent's voters are spread over many constituencies. They then remain a minority everywhere and win nowhere. In **packing**, the opponent's supporters are squeezed into a few constituencies. There the opponent wins by a huge margin, but the surplus votes are missing elsewhere.

Imagine 50 voters divided into 5 constituencies of 10 people each. 30 vote for party A, 20 for party B. To win, B needs at least 6 out of 10 votes. With clever division, B can therefore win **3 constituencies**, because 3 times 6 makes 18. Even though A has the **majority** of votes, B then wins more constituencies.

In the USA the House of Representatives is elected in constituencies with one seat each. After every **census**, every 10 years, the seats are redistributed among the states and the boundaries redrawn. This is called **redistricting**. It is often done by the state legislature. Some states, such as **California**, have an independent commission of citizens do this work.

In 2019 the US Supreme Court ruled in the case **“Rucho v. Common Cause”**. It declared that federal courts cannot review partisan gerrymandering. It said it was a political question. The states and Congress can, however, make their own rules against it. In Switzerland the constituencies for the National Council are the **cantons**, so gerrymandering is hardly possible here.

gewusst: Some constituencies in the USA look like long, winding snakes on the map.
The word gerrymandering is over 200 years old and is now used all over the world.

teile.einleitung: HarmoS is an agreement between Swiss cantons. It aligns important key features of compulsory schooling, for example the age at which children start school and the length of the school stages. The name stands for the harmonisation of compulsory schooling.
wichtigste: HarmoS is short for the harmonisation of compulsory schooling.
The concordat came into force in 2009, after ten cantons had joined.
15 cantons have joined; in seven cantons the people said no.
Children start school at four; the cut-off date is 31 July.
The two years of nursery school count too: 1H and 2H.
The cantons that have joined offer block timetables and day-care facilities.
National basic skills set out what almost everyone should be able to do.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **cantons** are responsible for schools. That is why schools were quite different for a long time. **HarmoS** stands for the **Intercantonal Agreement on the Harmonisation of Compulsory Schooling**. Such an agreement between cantons is called a **concordat**. It aligns important key features, so that moving to another canton becomes easier. It was drawn up by the **EDK**, the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education.

The concordat was to apply as soon as **ten cantons** had joined. The tenth canton was **Ticino**. So HarmoS came into force in **2009**. By the end of the implementation period in **2015**, **15 cantons** had joined. In **seven cantons** the people rejected joining in a vote. Some other cantons suspended joining or did not take it up.

Under HarmoS, children start school once they have **turned four**. The cut-off date is **31 July**: whoever is four by then goes to nursery school. This made **nursery school compulsory**. The two years of nursery school count too; they are called **1H and 2H**. The former 1st year of primary school is therefore **3H**, and compulsory schooling lasts eleven years, up to 11H.

The cantons that have joined commit themselves to **block timetables**. This means that lessons in the morning last the same length of time for all children. There is also a range of **day-care facilities**, for example a **lunch club** and care after school. Using these services is voluntary. This helps many families to combine work and family life.

In **2011** the EDK adopted national education goals in the form of **basic skills**. They describe what almost all pupils should be able to do, for example in the **language of schooling**, in **maths** and in foreign languages. Whether these goals are reached is checked by the **ÜGK**, the assessment of the attainment of basic skills. For this, samples of pupils are tested in all cantons. **PISA**, on the other hand, is an international study by the OECD.

gewusst: In 2006 Swiss voters approved a new education article in the Federal Constitution, which obliges the cantons to harmonise their schools.
In German-speaking Switzerland the Lehrplan 21 curriculum builds on the goals of HarmoS; in French-speaking Switzerland it is the Plan d'études romand.

teile.einleitung: The Control Committees, GPK for short, are committees of the Swiss Parliament. There is one in the National Council and one in the Council of States. They check whether the Federal Council, the federal administration and the federal courts are doing their work properly.
wichtigste: The Control Committees exercise overall supervision of the Federal Council, the administration and the federal courts.
The basis is Article 169 of the Federal Constitution.
They mainly check legality, appropriateness and effectiveness.
The Control Delegation supervises state security and the intelligence services.
The Parliamentary Control of the Administration supports them with evaluations.
The Control Committees work independently of party politics and aim for consensus.

abschnitte.titel: The task of the Control Committees
abschnitte.text: Under **Article 169 of the Federal Constitution**, the Federal Assembly exercises **overall supervision**. This work is done mainly by the Control Committees. They supervise the **Federal Council**, the federal administration and the federal courts. Other bodies that carry out federal tasks are also included. Every year the Control Committees examine the **annual reports** of the Federal Council and the federal courts, which the chambers then approve.

The Control Committees check three things above all: **legality**, **appropriateness** and **effectiveness**. Are the authorities keeping to the law? Is their approach sensible? Does it reach its goal? The checks usually take place **afterwards**. The Control Committees publish reports with **recommendations**, and the authority concerned must respond to them.

The **Control Delegation (GPDel)** is made up of three members from each of the two Control Committees. It supervises **state security** and the **intelligence services**. For this it has particularly extensive rights to information. It was created as a result of the **secret files scandal**: investigations in 1989 and 1990 had revealed serious gaps in supervision. The delegation met for the first time in March 1992.

abschnitte.titel: Support and comparison with a PUK
abschnitte.text: The **Parliamentary Control of the Administration (PCA)** is part of the Parliamentary Services. It carries out scientific **evaluations** on behalf of the Control Committees. The Control Committees have extensive rights to information. But a **Parliamentary Investigation Committee (PUK)** has even greater powers of investigation. That is why a PUK is only set up for events of great significance.

Members of different parties sit on the Control Committees. Even so, they work **independently of party politics** and according to the **consensus principle**. They aim to reach findings that are as unanimous as possible. Only in exceptional cases is an important minority opinion published. This is meant to make their reports credible and stop them being seen as party politics.

gewusst: The Control Committees of the National Council and the Council of States often carry out larger investigations together.
In the secret files scandal, it became known that state security had kept index cards, so-called “Fichen”, on many people and organisations.

teile.einleitung: Every Swiss canton has its own constitution. For it to apply, the Confederation must guarantee it, meaning confirm that it does not contradict federal law. The Federal Assembly is responsible for this.
wichtigste: Every cantonal constitution needs the Confederation's guarantee.
The Confederation must guarantee it if it does not contradict federal law.
This is set out in Article 51 of the Federal Constitution.
There is no political assessment.
The Federal Assembly's decision is final and cannot be challenged.
The guarantee has only very rarely been refused.

abschnitte.text: According to **Article 51 of the Federal Constitution**, every canton needs a democratic constitution. It must be approved by the people. The Confederation **guarantees** the cantonal constitution if it does not contradict **federal law**. So it only checks whether it fits legally. Whether it likes the content politically does not matter.

The **Federal Assembly**, meaning the National Council and the Council of States, decides on the guarantee. Its decision is **final** and cannot be challenged at the Federal Supreme Court. However, the Federal Supreme Court can later check whether cantonal law is being applied correctly in an individual case. The guarantee is **not constitutive**: it only confirms the law but does not create it. That is why a change can come into force beforehand.

In 1948 the Federal Assembly refused to guarantee articles of the cantons of **Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft** on reunification. It saw them as a violation of the **territorial guarantee**. In 1960 it reversed this decision. The canton of **Jura** also did not receive a guarantee for one article in 1977. Its first constitution planned to take in further areas of the Jura region.

In 2013 the canton of **Schwyz** did not receive a guarantee for its electoral system for the cantonal parliament at the time. The National Council rejected it twice, because the system violated **equal voting rights**. Small constituencies meant that not all votes carried the same weight. Schwyz then introduced the **double Pukelsheim**, a method for a fairer distribution of seats.

If the guarantee is refused, the provision lapses **retroactively**, back to the date it came into force. The canton must then change it. But such cases are very rare. According to the **Parliamentary Services**, the guarantee has only been refused in **five cases** so far (as of 2026). In almost all other cases it was granted.

gewusst: Every year cantons submit changes to their constitutions to the Confederation for guarantee, usually without any discussion.
The double Pukelsheim is named after the German mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim.

teile.einleitung: The mayor is at the head of a municipality. In many Swiss municipalities they lead the municipal government and are something like the face of the village or town. Whoever holds this office deals with very local things such as school buildings, roads, water and festivals.
wichtigste: The mayor leads the municipal government, the municipal council.
The office is part of the municipality's executive, meaning the authority that carries out decisions.
In most municipalities the person is elected directly by the voters.
In towns the office is usually called town president.
Depending on the canton there are other names, for example Gemeindeammann, Syndic, Maire or Sindaco.
In small municipalities the office is often a part-time role done alongside a job.
The mayor represents the municipality to the outside world, for example towards the canton.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has around 2100 **municipalities**, and each one needs leadership. The mayor chairs the meetings of the **municipal council**, the municipal government. Together with the other members of this body, they run the municipality's business. The office is the highest post in the municipality, but the person cannot decide alone.

Usually the municipality's **voters** elect the mayor directly at the ballot box. In some municipalities the election takes place at the municipal assembly. Depending on the canton, a term of office usually lasts four or five years. After that, you can stand for election again.

Together with the municipal council, the mayor prepares business, for example the **budget** or the building of a new school. In municipalities with a municipal assembly, the mayor often chairs it. They work closely with the municipal administration and the municipal clerk. They also welcome guests, give speeches at the National Day celebration on 1 August and sometimes congratulate very old people on their birthday.

In the canton of Aargau the office is called **Gemeindeammann**. In the French-speaking cantons of Vaud and Fribourg people say Syndic, in Geneva, Neuchâtel and the Jura Maire. In Ticino the person is called Sindaco or Sindaca. In big cities such as Zurich, Bern or Basel people speak of the **town president**, and in Basel of the president of the government, because the city is also a canton there.

In small villages the office is a **militia office**. This means that the person also has a normal job, for example as a farmer, teacher or tradesperson. In larger towns, on the other hand, the post is a full-time job with a proper salary. Some municipalities now find it hard to find people willing to take on such an office.

Hardly any politician is as close to the people as a mayor. You meet them in the shop, at the village festival or on the way to school and can speak to them directly. Many well-known politicians began their career in a **municipality**. That is why the office is a school for democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The government of a municipality, with several members. In some big cities, however, this name is used for the municipal parliament.
The authority that carries out decisions and governs.
A political office that you hold alongside your actual job.
The period for which someone is elected to an office.

gewusst: In the city of Zurich the town government is called the Stadtrat, while the town parliament is called the Gemeinderat, exactly the other way round from many villages.
Because the municipality of Basel and the canton of Basel-Stadt are closely linked, the city of Basel has no municipal government of its own.
Some very small municipalities have fewer than 100 inhabitants, but even there someone has to be mayor.

teile.einleitung: The municipality is the place where you live, and at the same time the smallest political unit in Switzerland. It takes care of many things you need every day: school, the playground, the roads and rubbish collection. There are around 2100 municipalities in Switzerland (as of 2026).
wichtigste: The municipality is the smallest political unit in Switzerland.
Switzerland has around 2100 municipalities (as of 2026).
The municipality often looks after the school, playgrounds, roads and rubbish.
It is run by the municipal council, headed by the mayor.
The municipal administration works in the municipal hall.
At the municipal assembly, those entitled to vote meet and help decide.
Large towns have a municipal parliament instead of an assembly.

abschnitte.text: A **municipality** is a village or town with its own administration and its own authorities. Switzerland is divided into three levels: the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. The municipality is the lowest level and the one closest to the people. Some municipalities have only a few dozen inhabitants; the city of Zurich has over 400,000.

The municipality often builds and maintains school buildings and nursery schools. It looks after playgrounds, municipal roads, parks and sometimes a swimming pool. **Rubbish collection** takes away the waste, and the municipality makes sure there is clean drinking water. It also keeps the register of residents, with which you must register after moving house.

The government of a municipality is usually called the **municipal council**; in some cantons it is also called the town council or municipal executive. At its head is the mayor, often called the town president in towns. In French-speaking Switzerland this person is often called the syndic. The staff of the municipal administration work in the **municipal hall**, or in the town hall in towns.

abschnitte.titel: Having a say in the municipality
abschnitte.text: Many smaller municipalities have a **municipal assembly**. This is a meeting that all voters may attend. There they vote, for example, on the budget, the tax rate or a new school building, usually by show of hands. Larger municipalities and towns have an elected municipal parliament instead.

The municipality raises its own taxes to pay for its tasks. That is why people pay different amounts of tax depending on where they live. Because small municipalities can hardly manage some tasks alone, many join together. These **municipal mergers** are the reason why there are far fewer municipalities today than in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: The government of the municipality, which runs its day-to-day business.
A meeting of voters at which municipal questions are decided.
A number that sets how high the municipal taxes are.
Two or more municipalities join together to form a new municipality.

gewusst: Around 1850 there were still over 3000 municipalities in Switzerland.
In 2011 the canton of Glarus merged its 25 municipalities into just three large ones.
Every Swiss person has a place of origin, a municipality whose citizenship they hold.

teile.einleitung: At a municipal assembly, the voters of a municipality decide directly on its business. Instead of electing representatives, citizens come to a hall themselves and vote by raising their hands. This form of direct democracy is typical of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The municipal assembly is the meeting of a municipality's voters.
In many municipalities it is the highest body, the municipality's legislature.
Voting is usually open, by raising hands.
Only people entitled to vote may take part, not all inhabitants.
Typical business includes the budget, the tax rate, the annual accounts and big building projects.
Most small and medium-sized Swiss municipalities have a municipal assembly.
Larger towns have an elected municipal parliament instead.

abschnitte.text: The **municipal assembly** is a meeting at which all the voters of a municipality may have their say and help decide. It is a form of **direct democracy**, because people decide themselves and not through elected representatives. It usually takes place in the gym, the municipal hall or the multi-purpose hall. It is something like the municipality's parliament.

Those who may take part are **people entitled to vote**, usually Swiss citizens aged 18 or over who live in the municipality. In some cantons, for example Neuchâtel, Jura, Vaud, Fribourg and Geneva, foreigners may also vote at municipal level if they have lived there for some time.
